query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a moderate amount of aluminum into a refractory high-entropy alloy (either as a bulk alloying addition or via a surface aluminization treatment) will promote the formation of a continuous, slow-growing Al₂O₃ protective scale at high temperature, thereby significantly improving the alloy's oxygen resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy for structural use that, in its baseline composition, forms a noncoherent or porous oxide layer under high-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.intervention: Incorporate an optimized concentration of aluminum (by alloying or surface treatment) sufficient to induce selective oxidation to form an adherent alumina scale.
generation.conditions: Exposure at approximately 1100°C in air (21% O₂) for extended durations (e.g., 100 hours), conditions relevant for extreme-temperature structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a coherent, dense Al₂O₃ layer on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum preferentially oxidizes to form Al₂O₃, a thermodynamically stable and slow-growing oxide. This protective scale acts as an effective oxygen diffusion barrier, reducing further oxidation of the underlying alloy, thereby enhancing its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy, the aluminized variant will exhibit a thinner, more adherent oxide scale and lower overall weight gain, reflecting lower oxidation rates under the same high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: The untreated alloy forms a less protective oxide (which may be porous or poorly adherent), resulting in higher oxygen penetration rates and more rapid scale thickening at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: This protective effect is expected to be robust up to about 1200°C in air; at temperatures significantly higher, scale spallation or accelerated kinetics might undermine the benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aluminum concentration and processing method (bulk vs. surface treatment) may require further refinement, and microstructural variations could affect the efficiency of the resultant alumina scale.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one set of the baseline refractory high-entropy alloy and one set with the aluminum modification (either via bulk alloying or surface aluminization). Expose both sets to 1100°C in ambient air for 100 hours. After exposure, analyze the oxide scale thickness, composition, and adhesion.
measurements: Cross-sectional SEM/EDS to measure oxide scale thickness and uniformity
Weight gain analysis to determine oxidation rate
XRD to identify oxide phases (confirmation of Al₂O₃)
Scratch adhesion testing to assess scale integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-enhanced samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxide scale thickness and weight gain compared to the untreated samples, or if the scale is not predominantly composed of alumina, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

System: NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy matrix with in-situ formed TiC and Al2O3 reinforcement particles. Processing: High energy planetary ball milling for 39 h at 300 rpm with stearic acid as process control agent, followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1700 °C under 30 MPa axial pressure for 30 min. Test conditions: Room temperature compression tests at a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 on cylindrical specimens (4 mm diameter, 6 mm height).
